simple: someone gets hurt, or something important is damaged.
analogy: the bruise or the broken arm after a car crash.
precise: physical injury or damage to the health of people (some standards also include damage to property or the environment); the thing a safety analysis is ultimately about.
source: D1 of F11-18 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: something that could hurt someone if things go wrong.
analogy: a sharp corner of the dashboard in front of a passenger.
precise: a potential source of harm; for a robot, for example, a moving arm link that can strike or pinch a person; a hazard leads to harm only in a hazardous situation (a person within reach) followed by a hazardous event (the arm moves unexpectedly).
source: D1 of F11-18 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how bad the harm could be, combined with how likely it is.
analogy: a short slow trip on a quiet road against a long fast trip on a busy one.
precise: the combination of the probability of occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm; reduced by design, by safety functions and by other measures until it is judged tolerable.
source: D1 of F11-18 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part of safety that depends on a machine's own systems doing the right thing at the right moment.
analogy: seatbelts and airbags that act when something goes wrong, designed and tested to rules.
precise: the part of the overall safety of a system that depends on a safety-related system (electrical, electronic or programmable electronic, plus other technologies) operating correctly in response to its inputs; contrasted with safety achieved by passive means (padding, guards, low force by design).
source: D1, D2 of F11-18 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the machine whose dangers you are protecting people from.
analogy: the car itself, with its engine and wheels.
precise: the equipment, machinery or plant that gives rise to the hazards, together with its control system; the safety-related system acts on it to reach or keep a safe state.
source: D1 of F11-18 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one specific protective job, like "stop the arm if it goes too fast".
analogy: the airbag: one device, one job, for one kind of crash.
precise: a function, implemented by a safety-related system or by other risk-reduction measures, intended to achieve or maintain a safe state of the EUC with respect to a specific hazardous event; specified by what it detects, what it does, how fast, and how reliably.
source: D1 of F11-18 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the parts (sensors, logic, outputs, software) that carry out the safety functions.
analogy: the crash sensor, the airbag controller and the airbag together.
precise: a system that implements the required safety functions and is intended to achieve the necessary safety integrity for them; it may be separate from the control system or share parts with it, and every shared part must then meet the safety requirements.
source: D1 of F11-18 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the condition the machine goes to when something is wrong, chosen so that it cannot hurt anyone while it stays there.
analogy: the car stopped at the side of the road with the engine off.
precise: a defined state of the EUC in which the hazard under consideration is absent; entered by a safety function and left only by a defined reset; it depends on the hazard (for an arm holding a load, "power off" may drop the load). Same meaning as in F9-69.
source: D1 of F11-18 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a part breaks at an unpredictable moment, the way a light bulb burns out.
analogy: a tyre that goes flat on one day out of thousands.
precise: a failure occurring at a random time from one or more degradation mechanisms in the hardware (wear, ageing, stress, radiation); can be described by failure rates and reduced by redundancy, diagnostics and proof tests.
source: D1 of F11-18 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a failure built into the design, so it happens every time the same conditions occur.
analogy: a seatbelt that was designed too short for tall passengers: every one of those cars has the problem.
precise: a failure related in a deterministic way to a cause in the specification, design, manufacture, installation, operation or maintenance, which can be removed only by changing that cause; all software failures are systematic. Reduced by process (reviews, analysis, testing), not by identical redundancy.
source: D1 of F11-18 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one cause that breaks two protections at the same time.
analogy: two brake lines that run side by side, cut by the same stone.
precise: a failure of two or more channels or functions from a single shared cause (a shared sensor, power supply, design error, environment or maintenance action), which defeats redundancy that assumed independence.
source: D1 of F11-18 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the list of steps, from the first idea to the scrapping of the machine, in which safety is planned, built, checked and kept.
analogy: the car's life from design drawings to crash tests to yearly inspections.
precise: the necessary activities for safety-related systems over the life of a product, from concept and hazard analysis through requirements, design, verification, validation, operation, modification and decommissioning, each producing documented outputs.
source: D1, D2 of F11-18 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: listing everything about a machine that could hurt someone, in every way it is used, and judging how bad each one is.
analogy: Farid's list of ways a passenger can be hurt, written before any airbag is designed.
precise: the lifecycle activity that identifies the hazards, hazardous situations and hazardous events of the equipment under control in all reasonably foreseeable conditions (operating modes, life phases, foreseeable misuse), estimates the risk of each, and determines the risk reduction required; called hazard and risk analysis in IEC 61508 and hazard analysis and risk assessment (HARA) in ISO 26262.
source: D1, D2 of F11-19 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the different ways a machine is used (working, being taught, charging) and the stages of its life (built, moved, repaired, scrapped).
analogy: a seat used for sitting, folded for boxes, or taken out at the garage.
precise: a mode is a defined state of operation with its own behaviour and people present (automatic, teach, maintenance); a life phase is a period from transport and installation through use, maintenance and decommissioning; hazards are identified for every combination that can occur.
source: D4 of F11-19 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the list of hazards, kept up to date for the whole life of the machine, with what is done about each one.
analogy: Farid's list, with a column saying which airbag or belt answers each line.
precise: a controlled record of each identified hazard with its context (mode), risk estimate, required risk reduction, the safety functions and other measures that address it, their verification, and its status; versioned and updated on every change.
source: D1 of F11-19 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how badly someone could be hurt, how often someone is in the dangerous situation, and whether they could get out of the way.
analogy: Farid's three small numbers on each line.
precise: the parameters of a risk graph: severity (S) classes the worst credible harm; exposure (E) classes how often or how long people are in the hazardous situation; avoidability (A, called controllability C in ISO 26262) classes whether the people involved can avoid the harm once the event starts.
source: D1, D2 of F11-19 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a fixed table that turns the three numbers into "how much protection this line needs".
analogy: the company rule that says which crashes need an airbag and which need only a belt.
precise: a qualitative method that maps combinations of risk parameters to a required risk-reduction class (an integrity level in a standard; a course target CT0 to CT3 in this course); calibrated by whoever defines it, and valid only with that calibration.
source: D1 of F11-19 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: this course's own label, from 0 to 3, for how much protection a hazard needs.
analogy: a practice grading scale, not the real exam's.
precise: SS402's risk-reduction class: points = 2·S + E + A; CT0 for at most 7 points, CT1 for 8–9, CT2 for 10–11, CT3 for 12–13; defined by this course for teaching, deliberately not equal to any standard's integrity levels (F11-20).
source: C1 of F11-19 (course rule) and R1 of F11-19 (lab run) (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: go part by part and ask "how can this part fail, and what happens then?".
analogy: checking each piece of the seat in turn: the rail, the lock, the belt buckle.
precise: a bottom-up (inductive) analysis that lists, for each component or function, its failure modes, their local and system-level effects, and how each is detected and mitigated; finds single points of failure; complements top-down analysis.
source: D5 of F11-19 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: start from one bad outcome and ask "what would have to go wrong for this to happen?", again and again, down to single parts.
analogy: starting from "the seat slid forward" and working back to the worn lock and the missing check.
precise: a top-down (deductive) analysis that decomposes an undesired top event through AND and OR gates into basic events; yields minimal cut sets and, with probabilities for the basic events, a probability for the top event.
source: D5 of F11-19 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a smallest group of failures that, together, is enough to cause the bad outcome.
analogy: "the lock is worn AND nobody checked it": both together, and nothing less, make the seat slide.
precise: a set of basic events whose joint occurrence causes the top event, such that no proper subset does; a cut set of size one is a single point of failure.
source: D5 of F11-19 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a grade that says how reliable a protection must be, and so how carefully it must be built and checked.
analogy: the go-kart's brake rules versus the school bus's brake rules.
precise: a discrete level assigned to a safety function (or to the system or software element implementing it) from the risk reduction it must provide; it sets both quantitative targets for random hardware failures (where the standard has them) and the rigour of the measures against systematic failures.
source: D1 of F11-20 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: IEC 61508's grade, from 1 (lowest) to 4 (highest).
analogy: four classes of vehicle, each with stricter brake rules.
precise: one of four discrete levels in IEC 61508 for specifying the safety integrity requirements of safety functions allocated to safety-related systems; SIL 4 is the highest; each SIL has a band of target failure measures for low-demand and for high-demand or continuous mode.
source: D1 of F11-20 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the car industry's grade, from A (lowest) to D (highest), with QM for "normal quality is enough".
analogy: the same idea, written for cars.
precise: one of four levels in ISO 26262 (A to D, D the most stringent) assigned to safety goals from the severity, exposure and controllability of hazardous events; QM denotes no ASIL requirement; requirements and their ASILs are inherited by the elements that implement them.
source: D2 of F11-20 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: aviation's grade for software, from A (most critical) to E (no safety effect).
analogy: the rule book for the software inside the bus's brake controller.
precise: in DO-178C, levels A to E assigned to software from the most severe failure condition its anomalous behaviour can cause (determined by the system safety assessment); the level sets which objectives apply and with what independence; often called a development assurance level (DAL).
source: D3 of F11-20 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: is the protection needed rarely (and must work when asked), or is it working all the time?
analogy: an airbag (rare) versus the brakes (every stop).
precise: in IEC 61508, a safety function in low-demand mode is demanded rarely (the standard states a frequency boundary) and its target is the average probability of dangerous failure on demand (PFDavg); in high-demand or continuous mode its target is the average frequency of dangerous failure per hour (PFH).
source: D1 of F11-20 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the chance that the protection is broken at the moment it is needed, averaged over time.
analogy: the chance that the bus's brake has an unnoticed leak on the day a child runs into the road.
precise: the time-averaged probability that a safety function is in a dangerous failed state, and therefore cannot act, when a demand occurs; for a channel with dangerous undetected failure rate λ and perfect proof tests every T hours, approximately λT/2 when λT is small (derived in Layer 3).
source: D1, R1 of F11-20 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a full, periodic test that finds hidden faults in a protection that is not used day to day.
analogy: the mechanic testing both brake circuits on the machine and signing the sheet.
precise: a periodic test that detects dangerous undetected failures of a safety-related system so that they can be repaired, returning it (ideally) to an "as new" condition; the proof-test interval T bounds how long such a failure can stay hidden.
source: D1 of F11-20 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a fault that stops the protection from working and that nothing notices.
analogy: a slow leak in a brake circuit with a broken warning lamp.
precise: a failure that prevents the safety function from acting on demand and is not revealed by diagnostics; revealed only by a demand or by a proof test; its rate is written λDU.
source: D1 of F11-20 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many channels there are, and how many must agree to act.
analogy: a bus with one brake circuit, or two where either one stops the bus.
precise: "M out of N": N independent channels, of which M must act for the safety function to act; 1oo1 is a single channel; in 1oo2 either of two channels can bring the safe state, so both must fail for the function to fail.
source: D1 of F11-20 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the share of failures that hit both channels at once.
analogy: the stone that cuts both brake lines because they run side by side.
precise: in the beta-factor model of common-cause failure, the fraction β of each channel's dangerous failure rate that is assumed to fail all channels simultaneously; the rest, (1 − β)λ, fails channels independently.
source: D1 of F11-20 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a part of the design whose job is to notice a fault and react before it can hurt anyone.
analogy: the vigilance button, the brakes that clamp when pressure is lost.
precise: a technical solution implemented by electrical, electronic or programmable elements (or other technologies) to detect, indicate, mask or control faults or failures, in order to maintain intended functionality or to reach or keep a safe state; characterised by what it detects, its detection and reaction times, and its coverage.
source: D2 of F11-21 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a watchdog that is upset not only when a sign of life comes too late, but also when it comes too early.
analogy: a vigilance button that also complains if it is pressed twenty times a minute, because that is not a driver paying attention either.
precise: a watchdog with a minimum and a maximum time between kicks; a kick before the window opens or no kick before it closes trips it; catches a monitored loop that runs too fast (a timer misconfiguration, a loop that skips its work) as well as one that stalls. Builds on the software watchdog and kick source of F9-69.
source: R2 of F11-21 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: noticing that something is wrong (and stopping), versus carrying on correctly in spite of it.
analogy: a warning lamp that says "a brake circuit has failed" versus a second circuit that keeps braking.
precise: a detecting architecture (such as 1oo2 comparison) recognises a disagreement and moves to the safe state; a masking or fault-tolerant architecture (such as 2oo3 voting) continues to deliver a correct output with one channel failed, at the cost of more hardware and a voter that must itself be trusted.
source: D1 of F11-21 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: three helpers compute the same number; the one in the middle is used, so one wrong helper cannot change the result.
analogy: three passengers read the speed sign and the middle answer wins.
precise: a two-out-of-three architecture combines three channel outputs; for continuous values, mid-value selection (the median) tolerates any single wrong channel, and the spread between highest and lowest flags the disagreement for diagnosis.
source: R1 of F11-21 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: building the backup differently from the original, so the same mistake is not in both.
analogy: one brake that works with air and a second that works with a spring.
precise: the use of different means (algorithms, code written by different people, different sensors, different processors or compilers) to perform the same function, so that a systematic fault in one channel is unlikely to be present in another; reduces, but does not remove, common-cause failure.
source: D1 of F11-21 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how long after a fault the hazard can start, so how fast the protection must act.
analogy: the distance to the obstacle when the driver stops responding.
precise: the minimum time from the occurrence of a fault in a system to the possible occurrence of a hazardous event if the safety mechanisms are not activated; the sum of detection time and reaction time to the safe state must be shorter (ISO 26262 uses this term; IEC 61508 speaks of the process safety time).
source: D2, D1 of F11-21 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: when something breaks, either stop safely, or keep working well enough to get to safety.
analogy: the train's air brakes clamp (fail-safe); an aircraft must keep flying (fail-operational).
precise: a fail-safe design reaches a safe state on a failure and accepts the loss of function; a fail-operational design keeps a (possibly degraded) function after a failure because no immediate safe state exists, which requires fault tolerance, not only detection.
source: D2 of F11-21 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: comparing a reading with something else you know, to catch a sensor that lies.
analogy: the speedometer says zero but the trees are moving past.
precise: a diagnostic that compares a signal with an independent signal or with a physical model (two encoders, commanded versus measured motion, rate-of-change limits) and declares a fault when they disagree beyond a tolerance for longer than a set time.
source: D1 of F11-21 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: checking that you built the thing the way the plan said.
analogy: measuring the buckle against its drawing.
precise: confirmation, by examination and provision of objective evidence, that the outputs of a lifecycle phase meet the requirements set for that phase (by review, analysis or test); answers "did we build it right?".
source: D1 of F11-22 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: checking that the plan itself was right, so the finished thing really keeps people safe in real use.
analogy: crash-testing the whole seat with a test dummy, not only measuring its parts.
precise: confirmation, by examination and provision of objective evidence, that the safety requirements are adequate and that the system as built achieves the safety goals in its intended environment and use; answers "did we build the right thing?".
source: D1, D2 of F11-22 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a sentence that says exactly what a safety function must do, so that someone can test it.
analogy: "the buckle opens with one hand, but not by a child's push".
precise: a requirement derived from the hazard analysis that a safety function or measure must meet, stated so that it is verifiable (what, when, how fast, with what integrity); refined from top-level safety goals to functional and then technical requirements allocated to design elements.
source: D2 of F11-22 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: links that let you follow any safety requirement to the part that does it and the test that checked it, and back.
analogy: the seat's label leading to its design and its tests.
precise: the documented, bidirectional relationship between hazards, safety goals, safety requirements, design elements, code, test cases and test results; it shows that every requirement is implemented and verified and that nothing in the design or the tests lacks a reason.
source: D3 of F11-22 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: every test result says exactly which version of the robot and which version of the requirement it is about.
analogy: the test of the new spring counts; last year's test does not.
precise: the identification of each verification result with the configuration items it applies to (software build identifier, hardware revision, requirement revision, tool versions), so that evidence is valid only for the released configuration and becomes stale when any of those changes.
source: D1 of F11-22 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: did the tests make each yes/no decision come out both yes and no, and did each small part of the decision take both values?
analogy: testing the buckle both closed and open, and each of its two catches both pressed and not.
precise: decision coverage requires every decision (a Boolean expression controlling a branch) to evaluate to both true and false; condition coverage requires every condition (a Boolean operand without Boolean operators) to take both values; neither implies the other.
source: D3 of F11-22 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: for each part of a decision, there are two tests that differ only in that part and give different answers, so you know that part really matters.
analogy: showing that pressing only the left catch, with everything else the same, changes whether the buckle opens.
precise: every entry and exit point invoked, every decision taking every outcome, every condition taking every outcome, and each condition shown to independently affect the decision's outcome (in the unique-cause form: by a pair of tests in which only that condition changes); for N independent conditions at least N + 1 tests.
source: D3, R2 of F11-22 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the person who checks is not the person who built it.
analogy: Elena checks seats; the people who designed them do not sign her report.
precise: separation between the people (or teams, or organisations) who produce an item and those who verify or assess it, graded by integrity level in the standards, so that the same misunderstanding does not enter both the design and its check.
source: D1, D3 of F11-22 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a written explanation of why a machine is safe enough for a stated use, with proof for every reason.
analogy: the folder for the inspector, plus the sheet that says what it proves.
precise: a structured argument, supported by a body of evidence, that provides a compelling, comprehensible and valid case that a system is acceptably safe for a given application in a given operating environment; maintained over the system's life.
source: D6, D2 of F11-23 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a sentence the case says is true, like "the arm stops before power is cut".
analogy: "the brakes work".
precise: a proposition in the argument, stated so that it can be true or false, with an explicit scope; the top claim is the overall safety claim; sub-claims refine it.
source: D6 of F11-23 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how you break a big claim into smaller ones.
analogy: "I will show the car is safe by checking brakes, lights, tyres and airbags in turn".
precise: the inference that connects a claim to its sub-claims, for example argument over each hazard of the hazard log, over each operating mode, or over each safety function; must be complete (the sub-claims together imply the claim) under stated context.
source: D6 of F11-23 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the actual proof: a test result, an analysis, a review record.
analogy: the inspector's brake-test printout, not the receipt.
precise: an item (test result, analysis, review record, field data) that supports a claim directly; it must exist, apply to the claimed configuration, be of a kind that can support the claim (a simulation cannot alone support a claim about hardware), and show what is claimed.
source: D6 of F11-23 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: what the claim is about and what you take for granted without proving it.
analogy: "this car, driven on roads, by a licensed driver" and "the driver is not drunk".
precise: context defines the terms and scope of a claim (the system, the environment, what "acceptably safe" means); assumptions are statements accepted without support in this argument, which must be listed so that reviewers and operators can check them.
source: D6 of F11-23 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a claim the case needs but cannot support yet, marked openly.
analogy: the three open lines on Amaka's sheet.
precise: a claim deliberately left without support, marked as such with the reason and what is needed to close it; the top claim does not hold until every undeveloped goal below it is closed.
source: D6 of F11-23 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)

simple: someone who did not write the case reads it to find where it does not prove what it says.
analogy: Amaka with the folder.
precise: an independent examination of a safety case for validity (does each argument step hold?), sufficiency (is the evidence enough and of the right kind?), completeness (are all hazards, modes and assumptions covered?) and currency (does the evidence match the configuration?), producing findings that the authors must resolve.
source: D1, D6 of F11-23 (pending verification; dossier gate G1 open)
